hops.title: Pull your hands apart to boost your knee kick
hops.text: Sit on a table edge, legs dangling, and have a friend tap just below your kneecap with the side of a hand. Hook your fingers in front of your chest, pull hard outward, and have them tap again. Look for a bigger kick. Ernő Jendrassik described this in 1883, and why it works is still debated; one idea was that mental effort helps. In 2012 Steven Passmore and Paul Bruno found that a hard color-word task made no measurable difference, while the pull strengthened the reflex and got the leg moving about 34 milliseconds sooner. Pulling may ease an inhibitory brake on incoming sensory signals in the spinal cord.

sources.citation: Zehr EP, Stein RB. Interaction of the Jendrássik maneuver with segmental presynaptic inhibition. Exp Brain Res. 1999;124(4):474-480.

image.caption: Pulling hooked fingers apart can strengthen the knee-jerk reflex, though why it works is still debated.

hops.title: The human gene-count bet
hops.text: In May 2000, at a Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory bar, Ewan Birney opened a betting pool called GeneSweep: how many protein-coding genes does a human have? Over 460 people bet, guessing from near 20,000 to over 200,000, even though the roundworm *C. elegans*, whose adult hermaphrodite has 302 neurons, already had over 19,000 predicted protein-coding genes. In 2003 Lee Rowen took half the $1,200 pot with 25,947; the count has since settled near 20,000. Counting is hard: a 2011 annotation predicted 30,907 genes in one *Daphnia pulex* water-flea isolate; a 2017 annotation of another predicted 18,440, estimating roughly 7,000 earlier models appeared to be false positives.

hops.title: How a pigment gene reroutes a Siamese cat's visual axons
hops.text: A Siamese cat's dark ears, face and paws come from a tyrosinase gene mutation that makes the pigment enzyme temperature-sensitive, so more pigment is made in cooler areas. In the late 1960s Ray Guillery found the layers of its visual relay station in the thalamus rearranged. The same tyrosinase mutation changes how developing retinal axons sort where the optic nerves meet, so some axons meant to stay on their own side cross over. In 1971 David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel found that in the Siamese cats they studied, the map in each visual cortex extended about 20 degrees into the same-side visual field. Many Siamese cats are also cross-eyed.

sources.citation: Lyons LA, Imes DL, Rah HC, Grahn RA. Tyrosinase mutations associated with Siamese and Burmese patterns in the domestic cat (Felis catus). Anim Genet. 2005;36(2):119-126.
